title: Story tap at the Jazz Vespers and its musicians
summary: Green tells how he tap dances story tap for the service and names the musicians who play there.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: like to call him "True Student" to myself, you see, because he's a reverend. And my life was saved by a reverend when I was a child, see, because I didn't know nothing about the Swanee River, see. That's how I was baptized. But it was a different body of water. And, like the dark (unintelligible) you see, I wasn't -- I didn't know how to see the light in the dark at that time. But I eventually did.

So, anyway not to speak too much about me as a tap dancer, but I am a kind of an example of what I'm speaking of here about the Reverend -- Jazz Vespers, you see. See, he's John too, you know. He's -- he asked me to come down some Sundays, you know, and this is -- to kind of make his message more open, you know, and to outlet the freedom that the land of the free is all about, you see.

And so, I tries to tap dance for him. I tried to story tap, you see -- I call it because it's like we are supposed to read some kind of passions in the day's lessons each day, you see, especially on the day of rest, see.

I had got reinstated by Oral Roberts, you know. My aunt before she passed -- and she was a WAC. She took me out on Long Island there somewhere, and I had to become -- I got a badge from the revival, see, you know, about Oral Roberts, you see. He gives a person an authority, see, like an officer of religion, you see, an older man or whatever.
But Reverend Ginzo, he -- and the Jazz Vespers -- I

mean he does these summons in the services of God, you see, because he's -- I think he really is a true student, you know, which is -- one never knows, you know, where the roller will begin or end, be (unintelligible) you see. The rolling tide comes in as the tide goes out, right.

But I mean, see, like I tried to get down there on the Sundays, see, because he's liable to be anywhere. You could enlist with the -- if you keep up with these services, your jazz vespers, you see. And it seems to be growing, and I hope that a lot of student bodies will prosper themselves from this, because it's quite a few he has turned out, you know. I'm waiting to read about them. I keeps searching the copies and trying to read about someone that has became popular from the Jazz Vespers, you see.
Who are some of the other jazz musicians that he has at his church?

Well, he has one fellow there that's named Lewis, you know. He's a great pianist, you know. Stanley Turrentine used to play there. There's Matthew Gee. He's continuing to play there. Well, he just had some fellow named John. And John -- I can't think -- I can't remember his last name. But he also plays the piano. He plays several instruments.
